## My Reasoning

I've been working this land since I was small, helping my mother and grandmother before I could even reach the irrigation channels properly. I know Quzhou soil — it's flat, the groundwater is reachable, but summers get dry fast. My husband and two older children take work in town sometimes, so I manage most of the fieldwork myself with my mother-in-law's help. Eight mu isn't big, but it's enough if I do it right.

I keep 5 mu in the wheat-maize rotation — same land, wheat in winter, maize right after harvest in June. The other 3 mu I put in cotton. Cotton takes more of my time and costs more for pesticide, but it fetches cash in a way grain doesn't. I need both.

For wheat, I'll use the improved variety seeds I buy at the township supply station — better tillering and I get a few more jin per mu than the old seeds. I'll do rotary tillage after I pull the maize stalks in October, then broadcast base fertilizer before sowing. I irrigate four times: once before sowing to prep the bed, once in December before the ground freezes, once at jointing in April, and once at heading. Two pesticide passes — herbicide early and aphids late.

For maize, I direct-seed right after wheat harvest — no time to plough in summer heat. Hybrid seed, everyone here uses it now. Summer rains usually help but I'll pump from the well twice or three times if it stays dry. Fewer pesticides needed.

For cotton, I plough properly in spring before transplanting. Bt cotton hybrid cuts down on some pest spraying, but I still need to go out four or five times for bollworm, aphids, and spider mites. It needs four irrigations at least. More labor, but it pays.
